Subject: Residencypinning and failover implications - quick recap + asks

Alice — thanks for the call this morning. Quick recap and concrete next steps so we can scope an accurate design and SOW.

Summary of what we covered:
- Primary goal: ensure PHI/PII stays in the US for production workloads, with predictable cross-region failover for availability.
- Nexa wants a warm-standby model in EU/APAC for DR only; active traffic must remain US-bound except during declared failover windows.
- Backup retention: 90 days for application snapshots; audit logs retained 365 days but with PII redaction options.
- Logging: token-level request logs are currently stored for 30 days by default; we discussed a redaction pipeline and sample retention tiers.

Open questions / asks we promised to follow up on:
1) Do backups/snapshots remain pinned to the same region as runtime (and are cross-region copies encrypted & accessible only via customer KMS)? Please confirm encryption-at-rest + KMS key residency options.
2) If we enable cross-region failover, what is the exact sequence for data failover (RPO/RTO expectations, snapshot restoration steps, manual vs automated cutover)?
3) How do audit logs that include request metadata get redacted for PII before longer-term retention? Can we provide an example redaction policy?
4) For compliance: confirm whether we can provide a customer-managed KMS (HSM) + SOC 2 documentation specific to residency controls.

Attachments: I added the spreadsheet you shared to the thread and attached a short questionnaire for your security team (Nexa-Residency-Questions.xlsx).

- Backups: we need confirmation that daily snapshots will be stored in the US by default and that cross-region copies (for warm standby) are only created on-demand or on an SLA trigger. We cannot have continuous replication of customer PII out of the US without an explicit agreement.
- KMS: Can the customer bring their own key (BYOK) and keep the KMS in a US region? Our policy requires keys to be under our control for all PHI.
- Failover test: we want a documented test plan for an annual DR drill that demonstrates RTO < 4 hours and data loss < 15 minutes (RPO). Please confirm whether Redwood’s restore path supports that with your warm-standby approach.

Also, can you provide a short diagram or step-by-step failover runbook (we prefer runbooks over long prose)? If possible, please include the operator steps required to initiate and reverse failover, and the checks to validate data consistency.

Best,

Subject: Re: Residencypinning and failover implications - technical detail and runbook sketch

Alice — thanks for the clear asks. Below is a concise technical response and a short runbook sketch you can use for the DR drill. I’ve also attached a one-page summary PDF.

1) Backups & snapshot placement
- Default behavior: production snapshots and incremental backups are stored in the primary region (US - us-west-2) by default. Cross-region copies to EU/APAC are only created as a scheduled job or as part of a warm-standby configuration you enable in the account. Continuous replication of PII out of the US will not happen unless you explicitly enable replication.
- Encryption: all snapshots are encrypted at rest with KMS. We support customer-managed KMS keys (BYOK) scoped to the account. Keys can be provisioned in a US region and used for encryption/decryption (customer retains control).

2) Failover model, RTO/RPO guidance
- Warm-standby approach: a read-only replicated model is kept in warm state in the DR region (minimal resources reserved, model weights present, KV cache cold).
- RPO: with our snapshot cadence (every 10 minutes for active writes) you can expect RPO approx <= 10 minutes when using incremental snapshots.
- RTO: full traffic cutover (DNS + routing + cache warming) target is 2–3 hours in our tests; typical validated run in recent customers was ~90 minutes for a controlled failover. We’ll include a canary validation step in the runbook.

3) Runbook (sketch)
Pre-reqs: ensure snapshot job is configured to take incremental snapshots every 10 minutes; BYOK is configured and keys are present in the US KMS; test account has warm-standby enabled.
Step 1 — Notify stakeholders and pause scheduled jobs.
Step 2 — Verify latest snapshot timestamp and replicate snapshot to DR region (if not already present).
Step 3 — Restore snapshot into the DR project (automated restore job available; manual fallback also supported).
Step 4 — Start model serving in DR region with traffic gating enabled (no traffic yet).
Step 5 — Warm KV cache by replaying a small set of requests (can take 5–20 minutes depending on history).
Step 6 — Run canary tests (synthetic requests + correctness checks).
Step 7 — If canaries pass, flip routing (automated routing policy or manual DNS update).
Step 8 — Monitor logs and metrics for 60 minutes; if errors occur revert to primary and open incident.
Reversal: use the same snapshot/replication process to move state back to primary when it’s healthy.

4) Logs and redaction
- We provide a redaction pipeline that: 1) detects fields matching common PII regex patterns, 2) applies field-level masking rules, and 3) writes a redacted version for long-term storage. The unredacted short-term window (default 30 days) is limited to authorized roles. We will provide a sample redaction ruleset (attached) and an insertion point where Nexa’s DLP rules can be applied.
